name: Apple fruit water

card.summary: A mild fruit-acid botanical water in some creams; one formulation study and little else.
card.aka: Malus fruit water, apple fruit extract
card.note: Very thin evidence base; AHA-containing products can raise sun sensitivity.

quick.overview:
Apple fruit water is a water extract of apple used in cosmetics as a gentle source of fruit acids and polyphenols.

The sources reviewed contain only one cosmetic formulation study, so little can be said about its effects on appearance.
quick.mechanism: The studied extract contained about 3.5 percent alpha hydroxy acids, which act as chemical exfoliants, plus antioxidant polyphenols.
quick.risks: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they may increase sunburn likelihood.

lead: Apple fruit water is a water-based extract of apple fruit used in skincare as a mild source of fruit acids (alpha hydroxy acids, or AHAs) and polyphenol antioxidants. People use creams containing it for gentle exfoliation, hydration and a brighter, more even-looking complexion.[1][2]

The main dedicated study is a 2018 report in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science on a cream with 6 percent wild apple fruit water extract, said to contain 3.5 percent AHAs plus polyphenols, stabilized with biodegradable alkyl-polyglucoside emulsifiers. In small volunteer tests, skin hydration rose over 28 days and the skin's melanin index dropped after a week of use on artificially darkened skin.[1]

AHAs such as glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation. Mild irritation, redness and flaking are the most common side effects, and the FDA has advised that AHAs can increase sensitivity to sunlight.[2]

chain: Water extract supplies mild fruit acids and polyphenols
angle.text: Apple fruit water supplies fruit acids that loosen dead surface cells and polyphenols with antioxidant activity, so creams containing it aim for smoother, better-hydrated, more even-toned skin. In the one volunteer study, hydration and melanin readings moved in that direction.

infobox: AHAs (3.5% in the studied extract), polyphenols [1]

paras: The extract described in the 2018 study was a water extract of wild apple fruit, incorporated into an emulsion cream at 6 percent.[1] The cream was characterized for appearance, pH, conductivity and antioxidant activity over 180 days of storage, and then tested on volunteers.[1]

AHAs, which include glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid, are used for chemical exfoliation of the skin.[2] The FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel consider AHAs safe at low concentrations, at pH above 3.5, with safety instructions, and the FDA has advised caution about sun exposure.[2]

Apple extracts appear in moisturizers and brightening creams as a fruit-derived alternative to synthetic exfoliating acids. Product claims centre on softness, hydration and a more even tone, which match the parameters measured in the 2018 formulation study.[1]

The 2018 formulation study combined laboratory characterization with small volunteer tests. The cream showed no irritation under 24-hour occlusion in 12 volunteers. In 10 volunteers using it for 28 days, skin hydration rose at 14 and 28 days while water loss and skin pH did not change. In 10 volunteers using it for 7 days on artificially darkened skin, the melanin index decreased, which the authors read as a lightening effect.[1] The authors concluded the cream was stable and safe in their testing and potentially useful for oxidative stress protection, dry skin and hyperpigmentation; sample sizes were small.[1]

No independent human trial of apple fruit water as a skincare ingredient was found. Registered trials that mention apples concern food or juice intake, such as glycemic response and cardiometabolic markers, and do not concern skin.

timeline.event: A cream with 6% wild apple fruit water extract is characterized in vitro and tested on volunteers.[1]
